text: The phone in your pocket. The AI you talk to. Both depend on five places on Earth.
Five places? That's all?
Five chokepoints. A small town in America. Two factories in a war zone. One Dutch machine. One British company. And one island.
Break any one of them, and the whole tech world feels it.
Then let's follow a chip all the way back to where it starts.
It starts... with sand. Well, very special sand.
Almost every chip is cut from a near-perfect crystal of silicon.
To grow that crystal, factories melt silicon at over fourteen hundred degrees, inside a bowl made of quartz.
Why does the bowl matter?
At that heat, the bowl touches the molten silicon. If the quartz has impurities, they leak in, and the crystal is ruined.
So chipmakers need quartz that is almost perfectly pure. And most of it comes from here: Spruce Pine, North Carolina.
Analysts estimate this one mountain town supplies around eighty percent of the world's high-purity quartz.
Who digs it up?
Only two companies: Sibelco, from Belgium, and The Quartz Corp.
Has anything ever gone wrong?
On the twenty-seventh of September, twenty twenty-four, Hurricane Helene hit. Roads, railways and power lines were cut. Both mines shut down.
The whole chip industry was suddenly watching one flooded valley.
Sibelco restarted about two weeks later. The Quartz Corp took longer.
Can't they find quartz somewhere else?
There are deposits in Brazil, Russia and China, and quartz can even be made synthetically. But nothing matches Spruce Pine's purity at scale... yet.
So the crystal is grown. But a crystal is just a blank. To draw circuits on it, you need light.
Light? How do you draw with light?
A chipmaking machine shines a laser through a stencil onto the silicon. The light prints the circuit, a bit like a photograph.
Most of those lasers run on a gas mixture that is mostly neon.
Neon, like the signs?
Same gas. And before twenty twenty-two, about half the world's chip-grade neon came from Ukraine.
Why Ukraine?
Neon is a by-product of steel making. The Soviet Union built giant air-separation plants at its steel mills, and they captured neon.
After the Soviet Union fell, two Ukrainian companies purified it: one in Odesa, one in Mariupol.
Mariupol... the city that was besieged.
Yes. When Russia invaded in February twenty twenty-two, both plants stopped.
Did the chip factories stop too?
No! Because it had happened before. When Russia seized Crimea in twenty fourteen, neon prices jumped six hundred percent.
Chipmakers learned their lesson. They cut their reliance on Russia and Ukraine from most of their neon to under a third.
China built new neon plants. South Korea's chipmakers started making their own. And laser makers learned to recycle neon, again and again.
In twenty twenty-two, one supplier said prices rose up to five hundred percent... but not a single chip factory stopped.
Neon lasers can print very small. But for the smallest circuits of all, there is only one kind of light... and only one machine that makes it.
It's built by A, S, M, L, in Veldhoven, in the Netherlands. No other company on Earth can make it.
What makes it so special?
Inside, a drop of tin, smaller than the width of a hair, falls through a vacuum. A laser hits it once to flatten it, then again to blast it into plasma.
Fifty thousand times every second.
Each flash is hotter than the surface of the Sun, and gives off extreme ultraviolet light.
And that light prints the chip?
It bounces off mirrors made by Zeiss in Germany. They're so smooth that, if one were blown up to the size of Germany, its biggest bump would be a tenth of a millimetre.
The result: circuits thousands of times thinner than a human hair.
How big is this machine?
Big. Delivering one takes forty shipping containers, twenty trucks and three cargo jets. The newest version costs around four hundred million dollars.
In twenty twenty-five, A, S, M, L shipped forty-eight of them.
Who buys them?
More than half of all these machines work for one company in Taiwan: T, S, M, C, the maker of Nvidia's AI chips and Apple's iPhone chips.
And China?
China has never received one. In twenty nineteen, under pressure from Washington, the Dutch government let China's export licence lapse.
So China has to make its best chips with older machines, printing the same layer several times over.
The machine can print anything. But what it prints, the blueprint, often comes from somewhere else entirely.
Look at the phone in your hand. Its brain almost certainly runs on a design from a company that has never made a single chip.
How is that even possible?
Arm, from Cambridge, England, sells blueprints for processors. Apple, Qualcomm, Samsung and others license them, then pay a small fee on every chip they build.
Arm-based processors are in over ninety-nine percent of smartphones. More than three hundred billion Arm-based chips have shipped.
Where did it come from?
In nineteen ninety, the British computer maker Acorn teamed up with Apple and a chip company called V, L, S, I. They started with twelve engineers.
And now?
Now it's one of the most fought-over companies in tech.
In twenty sixteen, Japan's SoftBank bought it for twenty-four billion pounds.
In twenty twenty, Nvidia offered forty billion dollars for it.
Why didn't that happen?
Regulators in America, Britain and Europe worried Nvidia would control the blueprints its own rivals depend on. The deal collapsed in February twenty twenty-two.
SoftBank kept Nvidia's one-and-a-quarter-billion-dollar down payment.
A year and a half later, Arm went public in New York, valued at around fifty-four billion dollars.
And in twenty twenty-five, reports said Arm planned to raise its prices by up to three hundred percent over time.
So whoever controls Arm...
...holds the keys to nearly every phone. Blueprint, light, machine, crystal. Now they all come together on one island.
If Taiwan stopped making chips tomorrow, the world would lose around ninety percent of its most advanced chips.
Ninety percent? From one island?
Mostly from one company: T, S, M, C, based in Hsinchu.
How did one company get so big?
In nineteen eighty-seven, an engineer named Morris Chang had a strange idea: a factory that makes chips only for other companies.
Back then, chip companies mostly designed and built their own. Chang's idea let anyone with a design skip building a factory.
Apple, Nvidia, A, M, D, Qualcomm... they all became customers. Since twenty twenty-five, Nvidia is the biggest of all.
Today T, S, M, C takes about seventy percent of all the money paid to chip factories worldwide.
And Taiwan sits right next to China.
The Taiwan Strait is only about one hundred and thirty to one hundred and sixty kilometres wide. Less than a hundred miles.
Many people call Taiwan's chips its silicon shield.
Is anyone trying to make them elsewhere?
America is. T, S, M, C has pledged one hundred and sixty-five billion dollars for factories in Arizona.
Its first Arizona factory began making four-nanometre chips at the end of twenty twenty-four.
But in Taiwan, mass production of two-nanometre chips had already begun. The newest chips still come from one island.

So follow your chip back. Quartz from one American town. Light from a gas once made in a war zone. A machine only one Dutch company can build. A blueprint from Cambridge. And a factory on one island, less than a hundred miles from China.
Five places. Five weak links.
And that's exactly why the world's biggest powers are now fighting over them.
